title: Perfect joy (Little Flowers 8)
hookLine: Francis says perfect joy is being turned away in the cold and staying patient

cards: Winter, on a road in Umbria. Two friars are walking home to their little church, Saint Mary of the Angels: Francis, and Brother Leo a little way ahead. It is bitterly cold.

Every so often Francis calls out. Brother Leo, write this down: if the friars everywhere gave a great example of holiness, that is not perfect joy. If a friar could heal the sick and make the blind see, not perfect joy.
If he knew every language and every science, not perfect joy. If he preached so well that whole peoples came to faith, still not. Until Leo asks: then, Father, for God's sake, where is perfect joy?

teach.b: The story comes from the Little Flowers of Saint Francis. Here is his answer. When we reach Saint Mary of the Angels, soaked with rain, stiff with cold, muddy and hungry, we knock at the gate.
The porter comes out angry and asks who we are. Two of your brothers, we say. And he says, you're lying, you're a pair of tramps who go around stealing alms from the poor.
He won't open, and leaves us out in the snow and the rain until night.
If we bear that patiently, without grumbling, and think humbly that perhaps the porter knows us better than we know ourselves, Brother Leo, write that this is perfect joy.
Francis pushes further: if the porter comes back with a knotted stick, and we bear that too, thinking of what Christ suffered, there is perfect joy. Then he explains.
Everything on his list, the miracles, the learning, the preaching, is a gift from God, so there's nothing in it to boast about.

teach.h: A JOY A LOCKED GATE CAN'T TAKE.
teach.b: He quotes Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "what hast thou that thou hast not received?" The one thing we can offer of our own is to bear a hardship for love of Christ.

teach.h: WHAT HAST THOU THAT THOU HAST NOT RECEIVED?
teach.b: And he closes with Paul again: "God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." Francis isn't saying the porter is right, or that cruelty is good.
He's pulling joy apart from success and recognition. The joy he means is the kind a locked gate can't take away.

how: Franciscan friars, sisters and lay Franciscans read the story of perfect joy from the Little Flowers, and some return to it when they meet rejection or hardship.

o: the bliss of a miracle or a vision sent from God
the happiness of seeing your good work praised
a joy in bearing hardship patiently, for love of Christ

games.q: the road to the gate — tap the pairs.

s: Francis says perfect joy is working miracles
he lists miracles, learning and great preaching, and says none of them is perfect joy.
Francis says the porter was right to shut them out
he never says the porter is right. he says patience outside the closed gate is perfect joy.
Francis quotes Saint Paul to explain himself
"what hast thou that thou hast not received?" every gift is God's; bearing hardship for Christ is what we can offer.

games.q: you're Brother Leo. for miles, in the cold, Francis has told you what perfect joy is not. what do you do?
o: ask him, for God's sake, where perfect joy is.
tell him you're too cold to listen.
games.why: Leo finally asks, and Francis answers with a locked gate, an angry porter and a night in the snow, borne patiently.

practice: Bring to mind a recent no, a request turned down, and stand outside that door again for a moment, noticing whatever rises.

You don't have to push it away; just breathe beside it, the way Francis pictures standing in the snow, and let your shoulders drop. If you pray, offer that closed door to God; if not, just rest outside the gate.

wordCard.voice: Perfect joy. For Francis, not success or praise, but patience outside a closed gate, for love of Christ. Today's word.

orig.note: Italian, the language of the Little Flowers: perfect joy, perfect gladness.

carryVoice: Your line: perfect joy. Every gift on Francis's list was received; the patience was his to give. Rest well.
